result.summary: Hesiod finishes his advice on sailing, warning against risky spring voyages and urging moderation in cargo. He then gives rules for marriage, friendship, speech, ritual purity and taboos, ends with a note on Talk, and begins listing lucky and unlucky days of the month.

scenes.title: Spring sailing and moderation
scenes.summary: Hesiod describes the spring sailing season but disapproves of it, and advises carrying only part of one's goods.
scenes.stakes: A sailor risks death at sea and loss of his goods.

scenes.title: Marriage, friends and speech
scenes.summary: Advice on the right age and choice of a wife, on dealing with friends, and on guarding one's tongue.
scenes.stakes: A man's household, reputation and friendships depend on prudent choices.

scenes.title: Ritual rules and taboos
scenes.summary: A list of religious and purity taboos, ending with a reflection on the divinity of Talk.
scenes.stakes: Breaking the rules brings the anger of the gods and bad luck.

scenes.title: Days of the month begin
scenes.summary: Hesiod starts the calendar of lucky days, naming holy days, good working days and the twelfth as best.
scenes.stakes: Working on the wrong days risks failure.

notable_quotes.reason: Hesiod's maxim of moderation, a famous Greek ideal.
Memorable claim that rumor is in some ways divine.

analysis.text: Hesiod stresses measure, prudence and reverence: a good life comes from avoiding risk, excess and offense to the gods or neighbors.
The taboos and lucky days preserve early Greek folk belief and ritual purity customs of farming communities.

legacy.text: The idea that moderation is best in all things echoes in later Greek ethics, such as the maxim 'nothing in excess'.

fun_facts.text: Hesiod's calendar of days is a rare early record of Greek lunar-month folk belief.

language_notes.text: Fig leaves the size of a cow's hoof-print mark the time; Hesiod uses natural signs, not a calendar, to time farm and sea work.
"Snatched" means a hurried, risky sailing grabbed before the season is safe; "mischief" here means harm or disaster.
"Hallow" means hollow, describing the hull of a ship.
"Roasts her man without fire" means a bad wife wears him down and ages him before his time; "raw" means premature.
"Do not lie to please the tongue" means do not speak false, flattering words merely to be agreeable.
The line means: do not let your expression show friendliness that your heart does not feel.
"Churlish" means rude, mean or ungenerous; "lavish" means wastefully generous.
"Boorish" means rough and ill-mannered; the advice is not to be stingy or rude at a shared meal.
"Spit them back" means the gods reject the prayers; the image is of prayers being refused like something distasteful.
"That which has five branches" is a riddling term for the hand; the rule forbids paring fingernails at a feast.
Setting the ladle on top of the mixing-bowl was believed to bring bad luck; the wine was mixed with water in the bowl and ladled out.
"Rough-hewn" means unfinished; a crow settling on it was an ill omen about the house's future.
"Uncharmed" pots are those not consecrated or protected by ritual, so they may carry some harmful influence.
"Make a mock of mysteries" means to treat sacred rites lightly; the translator renders a rule against improper behaviour at sacrifices.
Leto bore Apollo on the seventh of the month, which is why that day was sacred to him.
"The Wise One" is the ant, which gathers its store; the spider is mentioned as a sign of the day's industry.

context_notes.text: Sailing was dangerous and drowning feared, since death at sea usually meant no burial rites. Hesiod admits poverty drives men to the risk.
Hesiod advises men to marry near thirty. Greek men commonly married later than their brides, who were often in their teens.
Greeks believed gods allotted fortune, so mocking a poor man was to scorn what the gods had sent.
Libations were offerings of wine poured out to the gods, and ritual cleanliness of the hands was required beforehand.
Rivers were sacred and often thought to hold divine powers, so crossing them called for prayer and washing.
Talk (Pheme, rumour or report) was worshipped as a goddess; Hesiod's closing remark reflects that.
Hesiod begins a calendar of lucky and unlucky days of the month, which governed farm work and household tasks.

literary_notes.text: Overloading a ship is compared to overloading a wagon until the axle breaks, using a familiar farm image for sea risk.
The short maxim sums up the preceding advice in a memorable general rule, typical of the poem's wisdom style.
The wife who "roasts" her husband without fire turns the domestic burden of a bad marriage into a vivid image of consuming heat.
Speaking evil and being spoken of evilly are balanced, showing how one's own words rebound on oneself.
The short explanation about the nights belonging to the gods gives a religious reason for the rule, in a brief, proverb-like manner.
Talk is described as a being with traits, light to raise yet heavy to carry, preparing for the claim that she is divine.
The airy-swinging spider spinning its web in full daylight offers a vivid natural sign that the twelfth day is good for work.
